title: Serial Coincubation Enrichment Technique (SCET): Rapid isolation of bacterial biocontrol agents
author: Maheshwari, Gour, et al.

steps.title: Prepare mixed NB/PDB medium
steps.instruction: Combine 50 ml nutrient broth (NB) with 50 ml potato dextrose broth (PDB) to obtain a 1:1 (v/v) mixed medium, adjust volume as needed, and autoclave to sterilize.

steps.title: Inoculate fungal pathogen disc
steps.instruction: Using a cork borer, place a 10 mm disc of the target fungal phytopathogen (4‑day‑old Rhizoctonia solani or Sclerotium rolfsii, or 9‑day‑old Colletotrichum truncatum) into each flask containing the sterile mixed medium.

substeps.instruction: Incubate flasks in a shaker at 120 rpm, 28–30 °C for 24 h if the fungus is a fast grower (R. solani, S. rolfsii) or 48 h if it is a slow grower (C. truncatum).

steps.title: Add rhizospheric soil sample
steps.instruction: Add 1 g of rhizospheric soil collected from a healthy, disease‑free soybean plant directly to each flask that already contains the 24–48 h‑grown fungal culture.

substeps.instruction: Incubate the flasks for 5 days at 30 ± 2 °C.

steps.title: Serial enrichment transfers
steps.instruction: Enrich antagonistic bacteria by two successive transfers of the soil‑fungus suspension.

substeps.instruction: After the initial 5‑day incubation, transfer 1 ml of the suspension into a fresh flask containing fresh mixed NB/PDB medium that already holds a 24–48 h‑grown disc of the same target fungus.
Incubate this second flask for another 5 days at 30 ± 2 °C.
Repeat the transfer once more (third flask) with 1 ml of the previous suspension and incubate for a further 5 days under the same conditions.

steps.title: Serial dilution and selective plating
steps.instruction: From the final enriched flask, perform serial ten‑fold dilutions to 10⁻¹, 10⁻², 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁵.

substeps.instruction: Plate 100 µl of the 10⁻⁵ dilution onto nutrient agar plates supplemented with nystatin at 50 µg ml⁻¹ (to inhibit fungal growth).
Incubate plates and, within 24 h, select the unique bacterial colonies that appear (typically 1–2 per sample).
Purify each selected colony by streak‑plating on fresh nutrient agar.

steps.title: Set screening pH and temperature
steps.instruction: Adjust the assay conditions to pH 8.00 and maintain incubation at 28–30 °C to mimic the disease‑conducive environment for subsequent screening of the isolated bacteria.

steps.title: Biomass dry‑weight screening
steps.instruction: Strain the remaining broth from the final coincubated flask through Whatman filter paper, collect the solid residue, and oven‑dry it at 65 °C until constant weight is achieved.

substeps.instruction: Weigh the dried solid and compare it with the dry weight of a control flask containing only the target fungus grown under identical conditions; a significantly lower weight indicates the presence of antagonistic bacteria.

steps.title: Dual‑culture antagonism assay
steps.instruction: Test each purified bacterial isolate for antagonism against the target fungus using a dual‑culture assay.

substeps.instruction: Inoculate a bacterial colony on one side of a potato dextrose agar (PDA) plate and place a fresh fungal disc on the opposite side.
Incubate at 28–30 °C until the fungus has grown radially.
Measure the radial diameter of the fungus alone (D1) and in the presence of the bacterium (D2).
Calculate percent inhibition: % inhibition = [(D1 − D2) / D1] × 100.

steps.title: Additional antagonism assays
steps.instruction: Optionally evaluate the isolates for hydrocyanic acid (HCN) production, siderophore secretion, and cell‑wall‑degrading enzyme activities using the respective standard assays.

steps.title: Optional: Isolate antagonistic actinomycetes
steps.instruction: To target actinomycetes, pretreat 1 g of soil (physical/chemical), then coincubate it with 100 ml of a 1:1 mixture of nutrient broth and actinomycete‑specific broth that already contains a 24–48 h‑grown fungal pathogen.

substeps.instruction: Enrich as described in steps 4–5 (two successive 5‑day transfers).
Serially dilute the final broth to 10⁻⁵ and plate 100 µl onto starch‑casein‑nitrate agar amended with fungistatin (antifungal) to selectively recover actinomycetes.

steps.title: Optional: Isolate antagonistic fungi
steps.instruction: To isolate fungal antagonists, incubate 1 g of soil in 100 ml potato dextrose broth containing chloramphenicol at 50 µg ml⁻¹ and a 24–48 h‑grown target fungal pathogen.

substeps.instruction: Incubate for 5 days at 28–30 °C, then transfer 1 ml of the coincubated broth to fresh broth with the same conditions; repeat the transfer once more (total two 5‑day enrichments).
Serially dilute to 10⁻⁵ and spread 100 µl onto potato dextrose agar containing chloramphenicol (50 µg ml⁻¹) to suppress bacterial growth.
Identify fungal antagonists by morphology and confirm by microscopic examination; note that fungal biomass comparison is not a reliable screening metric for this case.

description: In the present study, we isolated three bacteria (RAB1, RAB2, and RAB3) from the Rhizoctonia solani pathogen grown in culture medium. Here, RAB 1 and RAB 2 showed antagonistic activity against the pathogen (Fig. 1). Fungal biomass was also significantly lower than that of Rhizoctonia solani grown alone, indicating that the bacteria present in the coincubated samples reduced fungal development (Table 2).Fig. 1Isolation of antagonistic bacteria against Rhizoctonia solani through Serial Coincubation Enrichment Technique (SCET).Fig 1 dummy alt textTable 2Fungal dry weight of the sole pathogen compared with the pathogen coincubated.Table 2 dummy alt textSampleRhizoctonia solani (g)Sclerotium rolsii (g)Colletotrichum truncatum (g)Sole pathogen0.440 ± 0.019a0.928 ± 0.065a0.405 ± 0.008bCoincubated0.359 ± 0.018b0.328 ± 0.039b0.436 ± 0.016ap- value0.0067<0.0010.043Where data shows (Mean ± Standard deviation, n = 3), followed by lowercase letters indicate statistically significant differences between treatments as analyzed using the Duncan Multiple Range Test (p < 0.05) through SPSS version 30.00. Similarly, we obtained one bacterium each from fungal media containing Sclerotium rolfsii (Fig. 2) and Colletotrichum tructatum grown medium (Fig. 3), and named them CR1 and CT1, respectively. Among these, the bacteria isolated from Colletotrichum truncatum did not exhibit antagonism against the fungal phytopathogen, indicating that they were neutral. Further, the fungal biomass of the coincubated showed a non-significant reduction when compared to the sole growth of the fungus.
